findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential hard-codes the provider id string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, the constant that this same PR removes from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction's old code. The provider-id string is now duplicated across two modules (server-spi-private and the factory in services); if the factory's PROVIDER_ID is ever changed or refactored, the IDE/rename tooling will not catch the literal in CredentialHelper and recovery-code creation will silently fall through to the local-DB branch (or NPE on getProvider returning null) for federated users.

[ADVISORY] The fallback branch (updateCredential returns false -> local createCredential) is completely unexercised by the new test, which only validates the userStorageCreated=true path. Any regression in the else branch (e.g. wrong provider id or wrong credential payload passed to createCredential) silently breaks recovery-code setup for users whose storage does not support the type; the only test added in this diff asserts the storage-supported path exclusively, so CI stays green while the fallback is broken.

[ADVISORY] Provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" is hard-coded as a string literal instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, which RecoveryAuthnCodesAction itself just stopped importing for the same purpose. Two sources of truth for the provider id: if the constant or provider id ever changes, this literal compiles fine but the fallback branch throws a runtime failure (session.getProvider returns null -> NPE on recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) only on the untested fallback path, compounding the coverage gap above.

[BUG] The test storage's recovery-code validation accepts any remaining code via anyMatch and never consumes/invalidates the used code, so the same code stays valid across repeated logins, diverging from the real provider's used-code rotation semantics. The backwards-compatibility suite validates weaker semantics than production: a regression in the real flow's code-consumption path (marking a code used after successful validation via updateCredential) will not be caught by this test, because the test provider always reports code 0 valid again on the next login.

[ADVISORY] The new test only covers the happy path: correct code entered once; there is no assertion that a wrong recovery code is rejected, and no second login to verify code rotation across the federated storage boundary. If the federated credential update after a successful validation (the mechanism that advances to the next code) regresses, users would be able to reuse the first recovery code indefinitely and the added test would still pass; the negative case (invalid code -> INVALID_CREDENTIALS challenge against federated storage) is also unverified.

[ADVISORY] The OTP tests include a full lifecycle coverage (setup through account REST, delete via account REST returning 204, re-verify absence) but the new recovery-codes test has no deletion/management counterpart, leaving federated recovery-code deletion unverified. Deleting a recovery-codes credential for a federated user via the account REST API (the path the OTP test at lines ~325-336 exercises) is an obvious sibling acceptance criterion that no test in this diff touches; a regression there (e.g. delete silently no-opping for federated recovery codes) ships undetected and users cannot remove stale recovery codes.

[BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user), throwing NoSuchElementException when the user has no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage. Any user who reaches a browser flow containing RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator without having configured recovery codes (e.g. flow assigned at realm level, user federated without codes) gets a 500/server error page instead of the login form or a graceful fallback, because the freemarker bean is evaluated during render.

[ADVISORY] The test storage's isValid() for recovery codes performs anyMatch over the full stored list and never removes consumed codes, so single-use semantics of recovery codes are not exercised by the new test. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin would still pass if real single-use consumption (credential deletion/invalidation after use) were broken, giving false confidence that federated recovery-code login matches production behavior; a regression in code consumption would ship untested.

[ADVISORY] This diff modifies BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, whose class javadoc explicitly states it is a Keycloak 4.8.3 compatibility provider that 'Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider'. Adding recovery-code support to a provider pinned to a historical version defeats the provider's stated purpose: it no longer verifies that old storage providers keep working untouched, and every future core change to recovery-code handling now requires editing this 'frozen' provider again. A purpose-built test storage provider would preserve the invariant.

[ADVISORY] The new test only covers the happy path (codes present, correct code entered); there is no coverage for the wrong-code path, exhausted-codes path, or a federated user without recovery codes reaching the recovery-code flow. The failureChallenge branch in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator and the NoSuchElementException path in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean (line 17) are untested against user storage; a regression that turns invalid-code attempts into a 500 or locks out users would pass CI.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes raw codes as a plain JSON list via UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson) into whatever user storage claims support, diverging from the local-storage representation produced by RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory (structured credentialData/secretData). Third-party user storage providers that claim the recovery-codes type (as the test provider does) will persist a representation that only the test provider's getCredentials() knows how to re-normalize; any consumer reading the federated CredentialModel directly and calling RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on it fails to parse, so behavior depends on whether the storage implements getCredentials — an undocumented contract the diff does not state anywhere.

[ADVISORY] The recovery-code validation compares input.getChallengeResponse() to raw stored strings without the normalization/hashing applied by the real RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider, and the unchecked raw List deserialization uses a raw type. The test provider accepts credentials the production validator would reject (or vice versa), so the integration test validates a weaker contract than production; formatting differences in user-entered codes would surface as failures only outside this testsuite.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes the credential through the generic user-storage updateCredential path as a UserCredentialModel whose challengeResponse is a bare JSON array of raw codes, bypassing the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider's canonical serialization (hashed codes wrapped in a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData document), creating two incompatible representations of the same credential type. Any consumer that reads a federated recovery-codes credential and calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel — including RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid and the account-console credential listing — receives credentialData that is a JSON array, not the expected credentialData document, and fails to parse/derive the real code list; the only reason the shipped test passes is that BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials hand-reconstructs the model from the raw list (a per-provider workaround that every other user-storage provider must copy or break), and the user-storage copy also stores plaintext raw codes while the local provider stores hashed ones, so the same credential type has divergent validation semantics depending on which store holds it.

[ADVISORY] The provider id is hardcoded as the string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, the constant the removed code in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction previously used. The stringly-typed id silently duplicates the factory constant; a rename or copy of this helper to another credential type drifts without compile-time detection, and the next author repeating the pattern has no single source of truth for provider ids.

[ADVISORY] getCredential changes the lookup precedence to federated-storage-first with local storage as fallback, so for a user present in both stores the federated credential silently shadows the locally stored one, and no code path in this diff reconciles or removes the shadowed copy. A user who previously set up recovery codes in local storage and is later moved to (or also exists in) a user storage that reports a recovery-codes credential will be validated against the federated copy — potentially a stale or plaintext-store copy — while the newer local credential is invisible; the dual-store ownership for this credential type has no precedence rule stated anywhere except this one method, so other readers (account REST, admin delete) can resolve the opposite copy.

[ADVISORY] The bean still calls Optional.get() on the credential lookup, so a user without any recovery-codes credential (federated or local) reaching this bean crashes with a bare NoSuchElementException instead of a handled empty case. Any flow misconfiguration or storage provider that claims support for the recovery-codes type without returning a credential sends users to a 500-style error page with no diagnostic message rather than a rendered login challenge; the diff rewrote this exact lookup and kept the unguarded unwrap despite now having the Optional in hand.

[ADVISORY] The test storage validates recovery codes by raw string equality against a plaintext JSON list, while the production RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates against hashed codes, so the new integration test exercises a stand-in validation contract that does not match the real one. The test suite can stay green while the actual production path for validating federated recovery codes (hash comparison, pepper handling, consumed-code accounting) is never exercised; a regression in the real validator's handling of user-storage-sourced credentials is invisible to this test.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes only the raw JSON array of codes as UserCredentialModel challengeResponse into user storage, discarding the structured credentialModel that the local path (recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) persists, so any storage that persists the CredentialInput verbatim produces a credential whose credentialData is a bare list instead of the format RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel parses. For user-storage-backed users (other than the test provider, which happens to re-wrap via createFromValues in getCredentials), RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns the raw model and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean/RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator call RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on it, which cannot parse the bare JSON list — recovery-code login fails or throws for real storage providers despite the PR's stated intent to support user storage providers.

[ADVISORY] The user-storage validation path validates a recovery code with anyMatch and never consumes/removes the used code, silently dropping the single-use semantics that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider enforces. A user authenticated via a user-storage-held recovery code can replay the same code indefinitely; the PR changes the security property of recovery codes (one-time use) as an undocumented side effect of routing storage through updateCredential/isValid instead of the credential provider.

[ADVISORY] getCredential unconditionally prefers a federated-storage credential over the locally stored one (or() fallback), whereas the pre-diff code in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator read only the local stored credential. If a user has a stale recovery-codes credential in federated storage and a newer one in local storage (e.g. codes were regenerated after the storage copy was created, or the storage provider stopped supporting the type after an earlier successful write), login and the code-display bean resolve against the stale federated copy and validate a code the user was not shown.

[ADVISORY] The new createRecoveryCodesCredential call hardcodes the literal provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" where the removed code used the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID constant. A rename of the provider id or a third-party override of the constant now silently resolves to no provider, making the local fallback path NPE (recoveryCodeCredentialProvider null) when user storage declines the credential — a compile-time-safe reference was downgraded to a string that only the test suite exercises.

[ADVISORY] The only new test exercises the user-storage branch (assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials + storage assertion); the local-storage fallback branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential added in this diff is never executed by any test in the diff. A regression in the fallback (e.g. the null provider from the hardcoded id, or a switch of updateCredential's return semantics) breaks recovery-code setup for all non-federated users — the feature's previously-working path — without any test failing.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials swallows the IOException with only a log line and returns the stream without the recovery-codes entry, so callers see 'no credential' rather than an error. On a corrupt stored credential, RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException during page rendering, surfacing a 500/server error at login instead of a diagnosable 'credential corrupt' condition.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential takes both credentialModel and generatedCodes, two parallel representations of the same codes that callers must keep consistent. The next caller can pass a credentialModel built from different codes than generatedCodes (or forget to serialize generatedCodes at all, since only the raw list reaches user storage while only credentialModel reaches local storage); the two parameters diverge silently with no single source of truth.

[ADVISORY] The user-storage recovery-code validator compares the submitted code in plaintext against a plaintext JSON list (JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class) then key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) and does not consume or invalidate the used code. Recovery codes remain valid indefinitely after use in this storage path, so a leaked or phished code can be replayed to authenticate repeatedly; this federated-provider pattern is shipped as reference code for vendors implementing UserStorageProvider, who will copy the non-consuming, unhashed comparison instead of the hashing/consumption behavior used by the built-in provider.

[ADVISORY] The .or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream...) fallback in getCredential is never exercised: the sole new test stores recovery codes only in user storage, so the local-storage lookup branch is untested. A regression in the local-storage lookup (e.g. wrong type constant or reversed stream order) would leave users whose recovery codes live in the Keycloak DB unable to log in via the recovery-codes flow while the new test still passes.

[ADVISORY] setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction supports logoutOtherSessions=false (uncheckLogoutSessions branch) but the only caller passes true, leaving that branch dead code in this diff and the logout-other-sessions=false behavior untested for recovery codes. A regression in the uncheckLogoutSessions UI path for recovery-code setup would not be caught; the OTP equivalent tests exercise both variants while the recovery-keys test does not.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only enters the single requested code (index 0) and has no negative-path case (entering an invalid/wrong recovery code and asserting rejection), so the userStorage-backed validation in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (lines 327-343) is never exercised for a failing credential. A regression that accepts any input (e.g. the anyMatch comparison degrading to always-true, or the deserialization-failure branch returning true) would pass this test suite; only the happy path of recovery-code validation is verified.

[ADVISORY] enterRecoveryCodes hardcodes expectedCode 0 at its only call site and never verifies subsequent codes or code-consumption behavior after a successful recovery-code login. The assertion 'Incorrect code presented to login' only validates the first login after setup; a regression that serves the wrong subsequent code index or fails to advance/consume codes after use would go undetected by the suite added in this diff.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes two incompatible on-disk formats for the same credential type depending on which store accepts the write: the user-storage path stores a bare JSON array of raw codes as credentialData (UserCredentialModel value), while the local path stores recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)'s RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel serialization, so the stored representation of recovery codes diverges by storage location. Any reader that deserializes credentialData in one format (e.g. the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials added in this diff reads it as List, while RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects the provider's own serialized format) throws on credentials written by the other path; users whose credential landed in user storage vs local DB behave differently and data written to one store cannot be losslessly moved to the other.

[BUG] When user.credentialManager().updateCredential() succeeds in user storage, any pre-existing recovery-codes credential already stored in the local Keycloak DB is left in place and never removed, because the code only ever writes the new store and reads (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential) preferentially from federated storage. A user migrated from local to federated storage accumulates two live credentials for the same type; the old local codes remain valid data that is shadowed on read but resurrected if the user-storage credential is ever removed, so removal of the user-storage credential silently reactivates stale codes that the user believes were replaced — a dual-write/cleanup gap that makes the transition non-reversible cleanly.

[ADVISORY] getCredential hardcodes the provider id lookup ordering (federated first, stored second) as the single source of truth for credential precedence, duplicated in spirit by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential's write ordering, with no shared constant tying the two together. If a future change reorders reads before writes are aligned (or a third storage location is added), reads and writes silently disagree about which copy of the credential is authoritative; during any backfill/cutover between stores this is exactly the state where the wrong copy is served.

[ADVISORY] The constructor still calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by the widened two-store lookup, so a user for whom neither store contains a recovery-codes credential crashes with NoSuchElementException when the recovery-code login bean is rendered. The diff expands the lookup surface (now also scanning federated credentials) without guarding the unwrapping, so any path that renders the bean for a user without codes — previously unreachable only if getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream was also empty — fails at runtime instead of degrading.

[BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without any presence check, so a user without a recovery-codes credential (in either federated or local storage) throws NoSuchElementException. Rendering the recovery-code login page for a user whose credential is missing (e.g. storage no longer returns it, or deserialization failure in the storage's getCredentials) surfaces as a raw 500/server error page instead of a graceful flow failure or 4xx-shaped response.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials() swallows the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery-codes credential with only a log.error, silently omitting the credential from the returned stream. A corrupted stored credential makes the credential silently disappear from credential listings and from RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential lookups (login then behaves as if the user never set up recovery codes) with no error result or surfaced state; the user's recovery setup is reported as absent rather than broken.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes two structurally different payloads depending on path: the user-storage path persists a raw JSON list of codes via UserCredentialModel, while the local path persists the structured RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel serialization. Any real (non-testsuite) user-storage provider that honors updateCredential and later serves the row through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel gets a payload it cannot parse, because only the testsuite provider was taught to re-wrap the raw list via createFromValues; future readers of this API must duplicate the test provider's re-wrapping logic to stay correct.

[ADVISORY] updateCredential() returning true is taken as proof the credential was created in user storage, but a UserRegistrationProvider may accept the write while persisting a payload its own validation path cannot consume, and there is no verification after the write. If a storage provider accepts the write but stores it in a form its isValid/getCredentials cannot round-trip, the required action reports success (reqActionContext.success() in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction) while the user is left without usable recovery codes — success reported while the work is effectively dropped.

goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential hard-codes the provider id string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, the constant that this same PR removes from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction's old code. adjudication.rationale: In CredentialHelper#createRecoveryCodesCredential the provider is looked up with a hard-coded string: session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes"). In the same diff, RecoveryAuthnCodesAction removes use of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID and delegates to this helper, so the single-source constant is no longer used here. This is a maintainability/architecture issue: the provider-id literal is now decoupled from the factory constant (defined elsewhere), so future refactors/renames of the provider id would not be caught by tooling and could cause getProvider() to return null or behavior to change (e.g., falling back to the local-DB branch). The diff does not prove an immediate runtime break today, assuming the literal matches the current provider id.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The fallback branch (updateCredential returns false -> local createCredential) is completely unexercised by the new test, which only validates the userStorageCreated=true path. Any regression in the else branch (e.g. wrong provider id or wrong credential payload passed to createCredential) silently breaks recovery-code setup for users whose storage does not support the type; the only test added in this diff asserts the storage-supported path exclusively, so CI stays green while the fallback is broken.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new branching logic in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`: it first calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` and only falls back to `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)` when that returns `false`. The only new test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) uses `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`, which was updated to support `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` and whose `updateCredential(...)` returns `true` for that type, and the test explicitly asserts the credential exists in user storage (`hasRecoveryCodes("otp1")`) and that there are no DB credentials. Therefore the fallback/local-storage `else` branch is indeed unexercised by the added test, meaning regressions in provider id/payload for the fallback could go undetected by CI.

Two sources of truth for the provider id: if the constant or provider id ever changes, this literal compiles fine but the fallback branch throws a runtime failure (session.getProvider returns null -> NPE on recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) only on the untested fallback path, compounding the coverage gap above.

In the same PR, `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` explicitly stops using/importing `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID` and calls into this helper instead, creating two sources of truth for the provider id. While the diff does not prove the literal is currently wrong (so a concrete runtime failure isn’t verifiable here), this change is a specific, diff-grounded maintainability/robustness concern because an id change would compile cleanly and could yield a null provider and subsequent NPE on the fallback path (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`).

The backwards-compatibility suite validates weaker semantics than production: a regression in the real flow's code-consumption path (marking a code used after successful validation via updateCredential) will not be caught by this test, because the test provider always reports code 0 valid again on the next login.

adjudication.rationale: The newly added test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only performs a single successful login using the first requested recovery code (`enterRecoveryCodes(..., expectedCode=0, recoveryKeys)`), and then asserts the app page is reached. It does not include a negative-path assertion (e.g., entering an invalid code should yield an `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` challenge), nor does it attempt a second login to verify the post-validation “next code”/rotation behavior across federated storage (the test only checks the credential exists in user storage via `hasRecoveryCodes`, not that codes are consumed/advanced). Therefore, regressions in code consumption/advancement or invalid-code handling would not be detected by this test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds recovery-codes lifecycle logic across storages (e.g., `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` attempts `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` then falls back to provider creation, and `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)` looks in federated then local storage). The newly added test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin()` in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest` only covers setup and login with recovery codes and asserts they exist in user storage, but it does not exercise management operations like deletion via the Account REST API analogous to the existing OTP test path that performs a DELETE and checks for `204` plus re-verifies absence. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in acceptance coverage for the new federated recovery-codes behavior, not a directly verifiable defect in the code itself.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the constructor now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. If `getCredential(user)` finds no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage, this will throw `NoSuchElementException` at runtime. The diff shows no guarding logic in this bean (unlike `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`, which checks `isPresent()`), so the finding is grounded in the changed code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test storage's isValid() for recovery codes performs anyMatch over the full stored list and never removes consumed codes, so single-use semantics of recovery codes are not exercised by the new test. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin would still pass if real single-use consumption (credential deletion/invalidation after use) were broken, giving false confidence that federated recovery-code login matches production behavior; a regression in code consumption would ship untested.

adjudication.rationale: In the new test-only user storage provider, recovery-code validation is implemented as `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` and does not remove/invalidate the matched code afterward. The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin()` in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest` only performs a single login with one recovery code and never attempts reuse or checks that the code was consumed. Therefore, this diff adds a federated recovery-code path where the test would still pass even if single-use consumption semantics were broken, making it a concrete test-coverage gap rather than a direct functional defect proven by the diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`, whose class-level Javadoc states it is an implementation “created in Keycloak 4.8.3” and that “Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider.” Yet this PR adds new behavior for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` throughout that provider (`supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential`, new `getCredentials` implementation, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`, and adds a `recoveryCodes` field), plus factory/test helpers. This is a real, diff-grounded scope/architecture concern: the provider is no longer “frozen” as an old-version compatibility artifact, and future changes to recovery-codes would require further edits here, weakening the intended invariant of “old provider works unchanged.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new test only covers the happy path (codes present, correct code entered); there is no coverage for the wrong-code path, exhausted-codes path, or a federated user without recovery codes reaching the recovery-code flow. The failureChallenge branch in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator and the NoSuchElementException path in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean (line 17) are untested against user storage; a regression that turns invalid-code attempts into a 500 or locks out users would pass CI.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new nontrivial user-storage logic for recovery codes (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential deciding between userStorage vs local provider; RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential checking federated first, then stored). The new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) only exercises the successful setup + successful login path with codes present. The diff still contains unguarded Optional.get() usage in RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean after switching to getCredential(user) (credentialModelOpt.get()), and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator has an explicit failureChallenge branch for invalid/missing input; none of these negative/edge paths are covered for federated/user-storage credentials. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage for newly added logic, not a proven defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes raw codes as a plain JSON list via UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson) into whatever user storage claims support, diverging from the local-storage representation produced by RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory (structured credentialData/secretData). Third-party user storage providers that claim the recovery-codes type (as the test provider does) will persist a representation that only the test provider's getCredentials() knows how to re-normalize; any consumer reading the federated CredentialModel directly and calling RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on it fails to parse, so behavior depends on whether the storage implements getCredentials — an undocumented contract the diff does not state anywhere.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` serializes `generatedCodes` as a plain JSON list and passes it via `new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)` into `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. That means any user-storage provider that returns `true` from `updateCredential` will persist whatever it interprets as `challengeResponse` (the test provider stores it into `CredentialModel.credentialData`). Separately, consumers were changed to read recovery-codes credentials via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)`, which prefers `user.credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` and then calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...)` on the result (e.g., `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). In the test provider, this only works because it newly implements `getCredentials(...)` to re-wrap the stored JSON list into a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` before returning it. The diff therefore introduces/relies on an implicit contract: third-party user storages must implement credential listing/normalization in a compatible way, otherwise the persisted representation from `updateCredential` may not match what `createFromCredentialModel` expects. The finding’s claim about divergence from `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory`’s internal structured format isn’t directly verifiable from this diff, but the mismatch/contract dependency is clearly grounded here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The recovery-code validation compares input.getChallengeResponse() to raw stored strings without the normalization/hashing applied by the real RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider, and the unchecked raw List deserialization uses a raw type. The test provider accepts credentials the production validator would reject (or vice versa), so the integration test validates a weaker contract than production; formatting differences in user-entered codes would surface as failures only outside this testsuite.

adjudication.rationale: In the testsuite provider `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)`, recovery-code validation deserializes `credentialData` with `JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class)` into a raw `List` (`List generatedKeys;`) and then does an exact `equals` match against `input.getChallengeResponse()` (`generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(...))`). This is a concrete, diff-visible divergence from any production behavior that might normalize/hash codes, so the integration test could be asserting a weaker/different contract than the real recovery-code validator. However, the diff alone does not prove what the production `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` does (hashing/normalization), so this is best treated as a test/contract fidelity concern rather than a verifiable product defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes the credential through the generic user-storage updateCredential path as a UserCredentialModel whose challengeResponse is a bare JSON array of raw codes, bypassing the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider's canonical serialization (hashed codes wrapped in a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData document), creating two incompatible representations of the same credential type. Any consumer that reads a federated recovery-codes credential and calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel — including RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid and the account-console credential listing — receives credentialData that is a JSON array, not the expected credentialData document, and fails to parse/derive the real code list; the only reason the shipped test passes is that BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials hand-reconstructs the model from the raw list (a per-provider workaround that every other user-storage provider must copy or break), and the user-storage copy also stores plaintext raw codes while the local provider stores hashed ones, so the same credential type has divergent validation semantics depending on which store holds it.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`, the user-storage path writes a `UserCredentialModel` whose `challengeResponse` is `JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` (a bare JSON array of raw codes), then calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. The diff also shows a federated provider (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential`) persisting that value directly into `CredentialModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())` and validating by deserializing the list and doing plaintext equality in `isValid`. Meanwhile, consumers were changed to prefer federated credentials via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)` and then call `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...)` (e.g., `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`). The test provider had to add a custom `getCredentials(...)` that reconstructs a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` from the raw JSON list, evidencing an incompatible representation for the same credential type between federated vs local storage and divergent (plaintext vs provider-defined) validation/serialization semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The provider id is hardcoded as the string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, the constant the removed code in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction previously used. The stringly-typed id silently duplicates the factory constant; a rename or copy of this helper to another credential type drifts without compile-time detection, and the next author repeating the pattern has no single source of truth for provider ids.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a hardcoded provider id literal in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`: `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")`. In the same PR, `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` removes usage of `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID` (imports deleted) and now calls this helper. This creates a single-use stringly-typed duplication of the provider id that would not be caught at compile time if the factory constant changes, making it a concrete maintainability/consistency issue but not an immediate functional defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential changes the lookup precedence to federated-storage-first with local storage as fallback, so for a user present in both stores the federated credential silently shadows the locally stored one, and no code path in this diff reconciles or removes the shadowed copy. A user who previously set up recovery codes in local storage and is later moved to (or also exists in) a user storage that reports a recovery-codes credential will be validated against the federated copy — potentially a stale or plaintext-store copy — while the newer local credential is invisible; the dual-store ownership for this credential type has no precedence rule stated anywhere except this one method, so other readers (account REST, admin delete) can resolve the opposite copy.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` which explicitly prefers `user.credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` and only falls back to local `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)`. Call sites in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` are switched to this method, changing behavior from “local-only” to “federated-first”. Separately, `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` attempts `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` (user storage) and otherwise creates a local credential, but it does not remove/reconcile an existing credential in the other store. From the diff alone, this makes dual copies possible and establishes an implicit precedence rule in one helper method, which can lead to surprising shadowing/inconsistency, but the diff does not prove which precedence is correct or that other APIs resolve the opposite copy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The bean still calls Optional.get() on the credential lookup, so a user without any recovery-codes credential (federated or local) reaching this bean crashes with a bare NoSuchElementException instead of a handled empty case. Any flow misconfiguration or storage provider that claims support for the recovery-codes type without returning a credential sends users to a 500-style error page with no diagnostic message rather than a rendered login challenge; the diff rewrote this exact lookup and kept the unguarded unwrap despite now having the Optional in hand.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, the diff changes the lookup to `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` but then immediately does `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. If the user has no recovery-codes credential (neither federated nor local), this will throw `NoSuchElementException` and crash request handling instead of rendering a handled challenge/flow outcome. This is directly visible in the added/modified lines in that bean.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test storage validates recovery codes by raw string equality against a plaintext JSON list, while the production RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates against hashed codes, so the new integration test exercises a stand-in validation contract that does not match the real one. The test suite can stay green while the actual production path for validating federated recovery codes (hash comparison, pepper handling, consumed-code accounting) is never exercised; a regression in the real validator's handling of user-storage-sourced credentials is invisible to this test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the test user-storage provider stores recovery codes as a plaintext JSON list and validates by raw string equality. In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential(...)` it persists `input.getChallengeResponse()` into `CredentialModel.credentialData`, and `isValid(...)` deserializes that JSON list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. The helper `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` constructs a `UserCredentialModel` whose `challengeResponse` is the JSON serialization of `generatedCodes`, so federated storage ends up with raw codes. The new integration test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) therefore exercises this simplified federated validation path; any production-specific validation behavior (e.g., hashing/pepper/consumption semantics) is not demonstrably exercised by this test when the credential is sourced from user storage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes only the raw JSON array of codes as UserCredentialModel challengeResponse into user storage, discarding the structured credentialModel that the local path (recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) persists, so any storage that persists the CredentialInput verbatim produces a credential whose credentialData is a bare list instead of the format RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel parses. For user-storage-backed users (other than the test provider, which happens to re-wrap via createFromValues in getCredentials), RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns the raw model and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean/RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator call RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on it, which cannot parse the bare JSON list — recovery-code login fails or throws for real storage providers despite the PR's stated intent to support user storage providers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` serializes `generatedCodes` to a JSON array string and passes it as the `UserCredentialModel` challengeResponse into `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, and if that succeeds it does *not* persist the structured `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`. Downstream, the PR changes both `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` to fetch a `CredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` and then call `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...)` on it. The testsuite user-storage provider had to be modified to compensate: it stores the raw list JSON (`setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`) and then re-wraps it into a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` in `getCredentials(...)` using `createFromValues(...)`. That strongly indicates the raw JSON list alone is not the expected persisted shape for `createFromCredentialModel`, so real user storage providers that persist the `CredentialInput` verbatim (and don’t perform this re-wrapping) would return an incompatible credential and recovery-code login/UI parsing may fail.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The user-storage validation path validates a recovery code with anyMatch and never consumes/removes the used code, silently dropping the single-use semantics that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider enforces. A user authenticated via a user-storage-held recovery code can replay the same code indefinitely; the PR changes the security property of recovery codes (one-time use) as an undocumented side effect of routing storage through updateCredential/isValid instead of the credential provider.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds recovery-codes support to the user-storage provider used in tests (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`). In its new validation branch (`isValid(... )`), it deserializes the stored JSON list and checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, but never removes/consumes the matched code or updates the stored credential data. Additionally, `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` prefers storing recovery codes via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` (user storage) when possible, which routes recovery-code storage/validation through the user-storage path rather than the local credential provider. This makes recovery codes replayable for users whose recovery codes are stored/validated by user storage, contradicting expected one-time semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential unconditionally prefers a federated-storage credential over the locally stored one (or() fallback), whereas the pre-diff code in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator read only the local stored credential. If a user has a stale recovery-codes credential in federated storage and a newer one in local storage (e.g. codes were regenerated after the storage copy was created, or the storage provider stopped supporting the type after an earlier successful write), login and the code-display bean resolve against the stale federated copy and validate a code the user was not shown.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` which does `getFederatedCredentialsStream()...findFirst().or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst())`, i.e., it always prefers a federated-storage recovery-codes credential over a locally stored one when both exist. Both `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` were changed to use this method instead of reading only `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)`. The diff also adds `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` which writes either to user storage (`updateCredential(...)`) or to local storage (`provider.createCredential(...)`) but does not remove/overwrite the credential in the other store, making it plausible for both copies to exist. In that case, the new preference order can cause login/bean to resolve against an outdated federated credential instead of the up-to-date local one, breaking login or allowing old codes to remain valid longer than intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new createRecoveryCodesCredential call hardcodes the literal provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" where the removed code used the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID constant. A rename of the provider id or a third-party override of the constant now silently resolves to no provider, making the local fallback path NPE (recoveryCodeCredentialProvider null) when user storage declines the credential — a compile-time-safe reference was downgraded to a string that only the test suite exercises.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show a downgrade from a compile-time constant to a string literal: `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential` calls `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")`, whereas `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` previously used `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID` (imports removed and call replaced). The helper also does not null-check `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider` before calling `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`, so if the provider is not registered/resolvable under that id the fallback path can NPE. However, the diff alone does not prove the provider id will ever differ or be missing in the supported runtime (the constant’s value and registration conditions aren’t shown), so it’s a concrete maintainability/robustness concern rather than a verifiable newly introduced runtime defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only new test exercises the user-storage branch (assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials + storage assertion); the local-storage fallback branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential added in this diff is never executed by any test in the diff. A regression in the fallback (e.g. the null provider from the hardcoded id, or a switch of updateCredential's return semantics) breaks recovery-code setup for all non-federated users — the feature's previously-working path — without any test failing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds conditional logic in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` that either stores recovery codes via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` or falls back to `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)` when that returns false. The only new test added (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) explicitly targets a federated/user-storage scenario (`assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials()` and `assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage(true)`), and the updated user-storage provider returns `true` for recovery-codes updates, so the fallback branch is not exercised by any test shown. Therefore, regressions in the fallback path (e.g., provider id lookup or behavior when `updateCredential` returns false) would not be caught by the added tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials swallows the IOException with only a log line and returns the stream without the recovery-codes entry, so callers see 'no credential' rather than an error. On a corrupt stored credential, RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean's credentialModelOpt.get() throws NoSuchElementException during page rendering, surfacing a 500/server error at login instead of a diagnosable 'credential corrupt' condition.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage#getCredentials(...)` which catches `IOException` during recovery-codes deserialization, logs an error, and then returns a stream without adding the recovery-codes credential (`credentialModels` remains without it). Separately, `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` was changed to use `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` and still unconditionally calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` (no presence check). If recovery-codes data is corrupt/undecodable, `getCredentials` will omit it, `getCredential` can return `Optional.empty()`, and the bean will throw `NoSuchElementException` during rendering (500), matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential takes both credentialModel and generatedCodes, two parallel representations of the same codes that callers must keep consistent. The next caller can pass a credentialModel built from different codes than generatedCodes (or forget to serialize generatedCodes at all, since only the raw list reaches user storage while only credentialModel reaches local storage); the two parameters diverge silently with no single source of truth.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(..., RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel credentialModel, List<String> generatedCodes)`. Inside, federated/user-storage creation uses only `generatedCodes` (serialized into `recoveryCodesJson` and passed via `UserCredentialModel` to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`), while local Keycloak-DB creation uses only `credentialModel` (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`). The method does not validate or derive one from the other, so it introduces an API where two parallel representations can diverge silently if a future caller passes mismatched inputs. The current call site in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` passes both, but the inconsistency risk is real and grounded in the new method’s implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The user-storage recovery-code validator compares the submitted code in plaintext against a plaintext JSON list (JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class) then key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) and does not consume or invalidate the used code. Recovery codes remain valid indefinitely after use in this storage path, so a leaked or phished code can be replayed to authenticate repeatedly; this federated-provider pattern is shipped as reference code for vendors implementing UserStorageProvider, who will copy the non-consuming, unhashed comparison instead of the hashing/consumption behavior used by the built-in provider.

adjudication.rationale: In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)`, the new recovery-codes branch deserializes a plaintext JSON `List` from `storedRecoveryKeys.getCredentialData()` and validates via `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` without consuming/removing the matched code or updating storage. This makes codes replayable (not one-time) on the federated/user-storage path. Additionally, `updateCredential(...)` stores the JSON in `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`, i.e., unhashed plaintext, matching the finding’s plaintext comparison concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The .or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream...) fallback in getCredential is never exercised: the sole new test stores recovery codes only in user storage, so the local-storage lookup branch is untested. A regression in the local-storage lookup (e.g. wrong type constant or reversed stream order) would leave users whose recovery codes live in the Keycloak DB unable to log in via the recovery-codes flow while the new test still passes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) which first searches federated (user storage) credentials and only falls back via `.or(() -> user.credentialManager().getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...))` to local DB credentials. The only new test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) sets up recovery codes through the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage provider and explicitly asserts the user has no DB credentials (`assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials()`) and does have recovery codes in user storage (`assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage(true)`). Therefore the local-storage fallback branch is not exercised by the new test, leaving that new logic path untested as the finding describes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction supports logoutOtherSessions=false (uncheckLogoutSessions branch) but the only caller passes true, leaving that branch dead code in this diff and the logout-other-sessions=false behavior untested for recovery codes. A regression in the uncheckLogoutSessions UI path for recovery-code setup would not be caught; the OTP equivalent tests exercise both variants while the recovery-keys test does not.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest, the helper method `setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction(String userId, boolean logoutOtherSessions)` contains a conditional UI path `if (!logoutOtherSessions) { setupRecoveryAuthnCodesPage.uncheckLogoutSessions(); }`, but in this diff its only call site is `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin()`, which invokes it as `setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction(userId, true)`. Therefore the `logoutOtherSessions=false` branch is currently unreachable in the added/modified tests and that UI behavior is not exercised for recovery-code setup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only enters the single requested code (index 0) and has no negative-path case (entering an invalid/wrong recovery code and asserting rejection), so the userStorage-backed validation in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (lines 327-343) is never exercised for a failing credential. A regression that accepts any input (e.g. the anyMatch comparison degrading to always-true, or the deserialization-failure branch returning true) would pass this test suite; only the happy path of recovery-code validation is verified.

adjudication.rationale: In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`, the test logs in and calls `enterRecoveryCodes(..., 0, recoveryKeys)` which enters only the requested/valid code (index 0 from `generatedRecoveryAuthnCodes`) and then proceeds to `clickSignInButton()` expecting success. There is no test case that submits an invalid recovery code and asserts `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` / rejection, so the new user-storage validation logic added in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` is only exercised on the success path. This is a concrete coverage gap for the newly added recovery-code validation behavior, not a functional defect in the diff itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] enterRecoveryCodes hardcodes expectedCode 0 at its only call site and never verifies subsequent codes or code-consumption behavior after a successful recovery-code login. The assertion 'Incorrect code presented to login' only validates the first login after setup; a regression that serves the wrong subsequent code index or fails to advance/consume codes after use would go undetected by the suite added in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` calls `enterRecoveryCodes(..., 0, recoveryKeys)` exactly once, and the helper `enterRecoveryCodes(...)` only asserts the requested code number equals the passed `expectedCode`. Since `expectedCode` is hardcoded to `0` at its only call site, the suite added in this diff validates only the initial post-setup login and does not exercise/verify code advancement/consumption or subsequent requested indices after a recovery-code login.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential writes two incompatible on-disk formats for the same credential type depending on which store accepts the write: the user-storage path stores a bare JSON array of raw codes as credentialData (UserCredentialModel value), while the local path stores recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)'s RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel serialization, so the stored representation of recovery codes diverges by storage location. Any reader that deserializes credentialData in one format (e.g. the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials added in this diff reads it as List, while RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel expects the provider's own serialized format) throws on credentials written by the other path; users whose credential landed in user storage vs local DB behave differently and data written to one store cannot be losslessly moved to the other.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the user-storage path serializes and stores `generatedCodes` as a bare JSON array string via `new UserCredentialModel(..., recoveryCodesJson)` and `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, while the fallback local-storage path stores `credentialModel` via `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. The diff shows these are different payloads for the same credential type (`RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`), meaning the persisted representation depends on which backend accepts the write. This is likely incompatible with readers that expect a specific `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` encoding (e.g., other code paths use `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...)`), and it makes credentials non-portable between stores / can cause runtime parse failures depending on where the credential was written.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When user.credentialManager().updateCredential() succeeds in user storage, any pre-existing recovery-codes credential already stored in the local Keycloak DB is left in place and never removed, because the code only ever writes the new store and reads (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential) preferentially from federated storage. A user migrated from local to federated storage accumulates two live credentials for the same type; the old local codes remain valid data that is shadowed on read but resurrected if the user-storage credential is ever removed, so removal of the user-storage credential silently reactivates stale codes that the user believes were replaced — a dual-write/cleanup gap that makes the transition non-reversible cleanly.

adjudication.rationale: The new `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` writes to user storage via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, on success, only logs (`if (userStorageCreated) { ... }`) without removing any existing local (Keycloak DB) recovery-codes credential. Separately, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` now prefers federated credentials and falls back to local (`or(() -> ...getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream...findFirst())`). From the diff alone, there is no cleanup path that deletes an old local recovery-codes credential when a federated one is successfully created, so a user can end up with both; if the federated credential is later removed, the old local one becomes active again via the fallback lookup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential hardcodes the provider id lookup ordering (federated first, stored second) as the single source of truth for credential precedence, duplicated in spirit by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential's write ordering, with no shared constant tying the two together. If a future change reorders reads before writes are aligned (or a third storage location is added), reads and writes silently disagree about which copy of the credential is authoritative; during any backfill/cutover between stores this is exactly the state where the wrong copy is served.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces an explicit precedence rule in two places: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` reads federated credentials first and then falls back to stored (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()...or(() -> getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream...)`), while `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential()` tries to write via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` (user storage) and only if that fails writes to local storage via `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`.
